question.problem: Given that $y=y(x)$ satisfies the equation ${y}^{″}-10{y}^{′}+24y=0,$ which of the following **cannot** be $y(x)?$
question.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-10\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+24{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +24) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +24 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation results in

$$
(\lambda -4)(\lambda -6)=0,
$$

and so the solutions of the auxiliary equation  are $\lambda =4$ or $\lambda =6.$

Therefore, any linear combination of the functions ${e}^{4x}$ and ${e}^{6x}$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only $4-{e}^{6x}$ is not a solution.
